title: Home Life
note: This is the excellence of living with a wife. It follows the chapter on righteousness because it is the first of the two states in which righteousness is done.

couplets.plain: The one called a householder is a steady support on the good path for the three who live as they should.
couplets.pm: The one called a householder, who lives in household righteousness, is a firm support on their good path to the other three: the student under vows with a teacher, the forest-dweller doing penance with his wife serving him, and the full renunciant. He gives them food, medicine and shelter, so that hunger, illness and cold don’t stop them.
couplets.note: The Tamil says only “the three”. He takes them as the other stages of life.

links.quote: The one called a householder
links.reason: Opens the chapter by naming the householder as a support for others.

links.quote: a steady support on the good path
links.reason: Makes the one at home the firm support of the three others.

couplets.plain: The one called a householder is the support of those who have renounced, those who have nothing, and the dead.
couplets.pm: The one called a householder is a support to those forsaken by their protectors, to the poor, and to those who come to him with no one and die. He stands as protector to the forsaken, so that they stay free of sin, and does what they need. He gives the poor food and more. For the dead he does water rites and the like, and sends them to a good world.
couplets.note: துறந்தார் normally means those who have renounced, as in chapter 3. He reads it as those forsaken by their protectors.

links.quote: The one called a householder is the support
links.reason: Lists those who have the householder to turn to.

links.quote: those who have nothing, and the dead
links.reason: Praises home life for standing by those who renounce, the poor and even the dead.

couplets.plain: The ancestors in the south, the gods, guests, kin and yourself: looking after these five is the chief duty.
couplets.pm: Keeping the righteous ways towards ancestors, gods, guests, kin and yourself is the householder’s chief righteousness. The ancestors are a class of god made by Brahma at creation, and their place is the south. Guests are new arrivals, expected or not. You count because righteousness needs you alive to do it. So a ruler’s tax is one sixth: five shares go to these.

links.quote: the chief duty
looking after these five
guests
links.reason: Third of the five: guests, set between the gods and kin.

links.quote: kin
links.reason: Fourth of the five: what is owed to kin.

couplets.plain: If your life fears blame and shares its food, your line will never die out.
couplets.pm: If you fear sin while earning wealth, and share it with those named above before you eat, your line never dies out in the world. If you share another’s wealth gained by sin, the merit goes to its owner, the sin stays with you and your line ends. That is why he says to fear blame.

links.quote: fears blame
links.reason: Promises a lasting line to the one who fears blame.

links.quote: shares its food
links.reason: Sharing food is the second condition of a line that never dies out.

couplets.plain: If home life has loving-kindness and righteousness, that is its quality and its fruit.
couplets.pm: If your home life has loving-kindness towards your wife and the righteousness of sharing with others, these are its quality and its fruit, in that order. Household righteousness can’t last unless wife and husband are of one heart, so loving-kindness is the quality and righteousness the fruit.

links.quote: that is its quality and its fruit
links.reason: Gives the test of home life: loving-kindness and righteousness are its quality and its fruit.

links.quote: loving-kindness
righteousness
links.reason: Beside loving-kindness, righteousness is named as what gives home life its worth.

couplets.plain: If you live your home life in the way of righteousness, what would you gain by going off on some outside path?
couplets.pm: If you lead home life by the path of righteousness, what more can you gain by going down the path outside it? That path of righteousness is fearing blame, sharing food and having loving-kindness. The outside path is leaving home for the forest. Home life brings more than that stage does.

links.quote: If you live your home life in the way of righteousness
links.reason: Speaks to someone who already keeps a home, and asks what more they could gain.

links.quote: what would you gain
links.reason: Holds that a rightly kept home leaves nothing to gain from another path.

links.quote: going off on some outside path

couplets.plain: The one who lives home life as it should be lived is first among all who strive.
couplets.pm: The one who lives home life with its proper nature is above all those who strive to give up the senses. “Those who strive” are those in the third stage of life, since those who have fully renounced have already let go. That stage has many forms, so he says “all”. The householder comes first because he gets the fruit without such striving.

links.quote: The one who lives home life as it should be lived
first among all who strive
links.reason: Ranks home life first among all who strive.

links.quote: is first among all who strive
links.reason: For someone weighing striving elsewhere against home life, puts home life first.

couplets.plain: A home life that keeps others on their path and doesn’t slip from righteousness has more endurance than those who do penance.
couplets.pm: A home life that keeps ascetics going on their own paths, and doesn’t itself slip from righteousness, has more endurance than those ascetics. It takes away obstacles such as hunger. Ascetics bear only the pain that falls on them, while householders also bear the pain of others.

links.quote: A home life that keeps others on their path
links.reason: Draws the model householder: keeping others on their path and not slipping from righteousness.

links.quote: has more endurance than those who do penance
links.reason: Rates such a home life above those who do penance, for endurance.

couplets.plain: What is called righteousness is home life, and it too is good if no one else can blame it.
couplets.pm: Of the two kinds of righteousness, the books name home life alone as righteousness. Renunciation too is good, like home life, if others can’t blame it for false conduct. It is hard, punishing mind and senses, while home life easily enjoys the five senses to the full, yet it is counted with home life only when it is that hard.
couplets.note: “It too” points back to home life in the plain reading. He points it at renunciation: that too is good, if it isn’t blamed.

links.quote: What is called righteousness is home life
links.reason: Says that what is called righteousness is home life.

links.remove: There is no ornament or jewel in the Tamil, which says only that it is good if no one can blame it.

couplets.plain: One who lives in this world as a life should be lived will be counted among the gods who dwell in the sky.
couplets.pm: One who lives on earth in the way of home life is honoured as one of the gods who dwell in the sky, though still on earth. He is sure to become a god later and enjoy the fruit of this righteousness. This tells the reward of home life in the next world. Its reward in this world is fame, told later.

links.quote: One who lives in this world as a life should be lived
links.reason: The promise is made to the one who lives as a life should be lived.

links.quote: counted among the gods who dwell in the sky
links.reason: Raises a life rightly lived to a place among the gods in the sky.

ideaLinks.reason: Home life has its quality only if it has loving-kindness.
Beside loving-kindness, home life needs righteousness for its fruit.
